etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English crabbe, from Old English crabba (“crab; crayfish; cancer”), from Proto-West Germanic *krabbō, from Proto-Germanic *krabbô, from *krabbōną (“to creep, crawl”), from Proto-Indo-European *grobʰeh₂yéti (“scratch, claw at”), a metathesised o-grade of *gerbʰ-. More at carve.

definitions.definition: A crustacean of the infraorder Brachyura, having five pairs of legs, the foremost of which are in the form of claws, and a carapace.
(uncountable) The meat of this crustacean, served as food; crabmeat.

quote.citation: 1959, Georgette Heyer, chapter 1, in The Unknown Ajax:
quote.text: But Richmond […] appeared to lose himself in his own reflections. Some pickled crab, which he had not touched, had been removed with a damson pie; and his sister saw […] that he had eaten no more than a spoonful of that either.

definitions.definition: A bad-tempered person.

quote.citation: 1983 April 30, Sue Hyde, “Expanding Worldviews”, in Gay Community News, page 12:
quote.text: She so obviously enjoyed every second of the concert that only the most stubborn crab could not have been warmed by her charm.

definitions.definition: (in plural crabs, informal) An infestation of pubic lice (Pthirus pubis).
(uncountable, aviation) The angle by which an aircraft's nose is pointed upwind of its groundtrack to compensate for crosswinds during an approach to landing; its crab angle.
(poker slang) A playing card with the rank of three.
(rowing) A position in rowing where the oar is pushed under the rigger by the force of the water.
A defect in an outwardly normal object that may render it inconvenient and troublesome to use.

quote.citation: 1915, W.S. Maugham, “chapter 116”, in Of Human Bondage:
quote.text: -- "I suppose you wouldn't like to do a locum for a month on the South coast? Three guineas a week with board and lodging." -- "I wouldn't mind," said Philip. -- "It's at Farnley, in Dorsetshire. Doctor South. You'd have to go down at once; his assistant has developed mumps. I believe it's a very pleasant place." There was something in the secretary's manner that puzzled Philip. It was a little doubtful. -- "What's the crab in it?" he asked.

quote.citation: 1940, Horace Annesley Vachell, Little Tyrannies‎[1]:
quote.text: Arrested by the low price of another “desirable residence”, I asked “What's the crab?” The agent assured me that there was no crab. I fell in love with this house at sight. Happily, I discovered that it was reputed to be haunted.

definitions.definition: (dated) An unsold book that is returned to the publisher.

quote.citation: 1844, Albert Henry Payne, Payne's universum, or pictorial world, page 99:
quote.text: […]  the unsold copies may be returned to the original publisher , at a period fixed upon between Christmas and Easter; these returned copies are technically called krebse or crabs, probably, from their walking backwards.  […]  A says to B, "I have had eight thousand dollars' worth of your publications, three thousand were crabs, that makes five thousand."

quote.citation: 1892, The Publishers Weekly, volume 41, page 709:
quote.text: […]  unsold copies and settling the yearly accounts; while for the publisher begins the much dreaded season of "crabs," as  […]

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To fish for crabs.
(transitive, US, slang) To ruin.

quote.citation: 1916, Ring W. Lardner, “Three Kings and a Pair”, in The Saturday Evening Post‎[2]:
quote.text: I thought at the time that that little speech meant a savin' of eight dollars, […]  But the Missus crabbed it a few minutes after her and Bess come in the room.

quote.citation: 1940, Raymond Chandler, Farewell, My Lovely, Penguin, published 2010, page 224:
quote.text: ‘Just so we understand each other,’ he said after a pause. ‘If you crab this case, you'll be in a jam.’

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To complain.

quote.citation: 1925, F[rancis] Scott Fitzgerald, chapter 7, in The Great Gatsby, New York, N.Y.: Charles Scribner’s Sons, published 1953, →ISBN, →OCLC, page 127:
quote.text: “The thing to do is to forget about the heat,” said Tom impatiently. “You make it ten times worse by crabbing about it.”

quote.citation: 1981, Stephen King, Cujo, published 2001, page 163:
quote.text: And if we do have to walk, I don't want to have to listen to you crabbing at me, Tad Trenton.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To complain about.

quote.citation: 2007, Douglas Newton, Dr. Odin, page 24:
quote.text: Well, because of this state of things they crabbed his scheme from the first, ridiculed it, wrote against it, spread broadcast a feeling of distrust.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To drift or move sideways or to leeward (by analogy with the movement of a crab).

quote.citation: 2000, Dana Stabenow, Midnight Come Again, →ISBN, page 251:
quote.text: Mutt stalked forward, matching him, step for step, crabbing sideways the way wolves do when they're going for the kill.

quote.citation: 2007, Pat DePaolo, The Beijing Games, →ISBN, page 454:
quote.text: The aircraft crabbed sideways in the cross-winds and leveled to horizontal.

quote.citation: 2015, Andrew Swanston, Waterloo: The Bravest Man, →ISBN:
quote.text: Another shouted order and again the squares crabbed sideways.

definitions.definition: To move in a manner that involves keeping low and clinging to surfaces.

quote.citation: 2011, Robert Vivian, The Least Cricket of Evening, page 108:
quote.text: Time slowed down then, became liquid in the aftermath of his grotesque, unfolding limbs; he crabbed his way down the faded line, rocking back and forth in braces he would use all his life.

quote.citation: 2019, Ronan Frost, White Peak:
quote.text: Foot by foot, he crabbed his way down another ninety feet of rock chimney until he stood on solid ground again, still very much alive.

definitions.definition: (transitive, aviation) To navigate (an aircraft, e.g. a glider) sideways against an air current in order to maintain a straight-line course.
(transitive, film, television) To move (a camera) sideways.

quote.citation: 1997, Paul Kriwaczek, Documentary for the Small Screen, page 109:
quote.text: If panning is not easy to make seem natural, crabbing the camera is even less like any action we perform with our eyes in the real world. There are a few circumstances in which we walk sideways:  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete, World War I), to fly slightly off the straight-line course towards an enemy aircraft, as the machine guns on early aircraft did not allow firing through the propeller disk.
(rare) To back out of something.

quote.citation: 1960, P[elham] G[renville] Wodehouse, chapter XV, in Jeeves in the Offing, London: Herbert Jenkins, →OCLC:
quote.text: “Nothing can possibly go wrong.” “Just as you say, sir. But I still have that feeling.” The blood of the Woosters is hot, and I was about to tell him in set terms what I thought of his bally feeling, when I suddenly spotted what it was that was making him crab the act.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English crabbe (“wild apple”), of Germanic origin, plausibly from North Germanic, cognate with Swedish dialect scrabba.

definitions.definition: The crab apple or wild apple.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: I prithee, let me bring thee where crabs grow;And I with my long nails will dig thee pig-nuts;

quote.citation: 1895, Robert Blatchford, “The New Party in the North”, in Andrew Reid, editor, The New Party Described by Some of its Members‎[3], London: Hodder Brothers, page 24:
quote.text: Just as by cultivation the acrid wild crab has been developed into the beautiful and luscious apple, may the unripe, ill-fed, neglected wild fruits of the fields and slums be developed into pure and noble and beautiful men and women.

definitions.definition: The tree bearing crab apples, which has a dogbane-like bitter bark with medical use.
A cudgel made of the wood of the crab tree; a crabstick.

quote.citation: 1741, David Garrick, The Lying Valet:
quote.text: She swore to such things , that I could do nothing but swear and call names : upon which out bolts her husband upon me , with a fine taper crab in his hand and fell upon me with such violence , that , being half delirious , I made a full confession

definitions.definition: A movable winch or windlass with powerful gearing, used with derricks, etc.
A form of windlass, or geared capstan, for hauling ships into dock, etc.
A machine used in ropewalks to stretch the yarn.
A claw for anchoring a portable machine.
(obsolete) To irritate, make surly or sour
To be ill-tempered; to complain or find fault.
(British dialect) To cudgel or beat, as with a crabstick

quote.citation: 1639, John Fletcher, Monsieur Thomas:
quote.text: Get you to bed, drab, courage Or l'll so crab your shoulders!

quote.citation: 1935, Jack Molyneux, John Fairfax-Blakeborough, Thirty Years a Hunt Servant: Being the Memories of Jack Molyneux, page 161:
quote.text: I was on a horse named The Skipper, a perfect terror to ride when he was in a bad humour, which he invariably was; nevertheless he was a splendid hunter and I never crabbed him.

quote.citation: 2021, H. De Vere Stacpoole, Vanderdecken:
quote.text: The Shiremans had a down on him over stores he'd condemned as not fit for dogs, let alone able seamen, and they'd got wind he was a socialist, and they crabbed him all over the shipping companies' offices.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Possibly a corruption of the genus name Carapa

definitions.definition: The tree species Carapa guianensis, native to South America.
(informal) Short for carabiner.
